parts.text: I am a medical doctor and researcher at

, where I am completing my PhD in epidemiology and paediatric endocrinology. My research focuses on the first 1000 days from conception, when the foundations of our health are being laid. What fascinates me is how much our bodies respond to their surroundings, even before we are born. I study the role of iodine and thyroid hormones in this early development, and what they might mean for children’s growth, brain development and health later on.
Before studying medicine, I studied Human Sciences at

. This background still shapes the questions I ask. I am interested in how our evolutionary history helps us understand our bodies, including why we are vulnerable to certain diseases. I am also particularly drawn to questions about women’s health, from thyroid problems to autoimmunity and the menstrual cycle, where there is still so much we do not know.

As a doctor, I want to be able to trust the evidence behind the treatments I prescribe, and know that patients can actually obtain them. Alongside my PhD, I therefore research and campaign for access to medicines and greater transparency in clinical trials, including with
. I look at how universities handle discoveries made with public funding, why medicines become unaffordable, and what we can do to change this. Through the
People’s Health Movement’s WHO Watch programme
, I have attended meetings of the World Health Organization in Geneva. I also cofounded the movement’s Dutch branch, De Gezondheidszaak.

I think curiosity is one of our most wonderful human qualities. As children, we ask endless questions, but many of us lose some of that curiosity as we grow older. Through my writing, I hope to encourage people to keep wondering about the world and asking how we know what we know. I write for NEMO Kennislink through

, a programme of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW), The Young Academy and NEMO. I want to show that science is a creative profession, one that allows you to keep looking at the world with a child’s sense of wonder.
